summary: Describes a standard method for storing Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) keys and signatures in the DNS, using the KEY and SIG resource record types. It was later updated by RFC 6944.

eli5.summary: This explains how to put one kind of digital signature and its key into the internet's phone book.

subtitle: How DNS stores a DSA public key and a DSA signature, using the KEY and SIG record types.

tldr.problem: DNS had been extended to carry keys and signatures, but there was no standard way to write a US Government Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) key or signature into those records.
tldr.mechanism: A DSA public key goes in a KEY record as algorithm number 3, built from a size byte T plus the numbers Q, P, G and Y. A DSA signature goes in a SIG record as T, R and S.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2536 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 6944. It notes that DSA key size is capped at 1024 bits and that DSA depends on good random numbers.

today: RFC 2536 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6944, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why DSA Needs a DNS Format
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the global hierarchical, replicated, distributed database used for Internet addressing, mail proxy and other information. RFC 2535 extended it to carry digital signatures and cryptographic keys, so DNS can be secured and used for secure key distribution.

RFC 2536 fills in one piece of that: how to store US Government Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) keys and signatures in the DNS. It assumes the reader already knows DSA and says that implementation of DSA is mandatory for DNS security.
sections.eli5: The internet's phone book can now hold secret-code keys and signed notes. This document says exactly how to write one particular kind of key and signature in it.

sections.title: The DSA KEY Record
sections.content:
A DSA public key is stored as a KEY resource record with algorithm number 3. The algorithm-specific part of the record data holds five fields, and the fields from Q through Y are the public key part.

  • T: 1 octet, a key size parameter with 0 <= T <= 8.
  • Q: 20 octets.
  • P, G and Y: 64 + T*8 octets each.

Q is a prime with 2^159 < Q < 2^160, so it is always 20 octets. P is in the range 2^(511+64T) < P < 2^(512+64T). G and Y are quantities modulo P, so they get fixed-size fields as long as P. Every field is stored in big-endian network order. If T is greater than 8, the meaning is reserved and the rest of the record may have a different format.

During key generation a random number X with 1 <= X <= Q-1 is chosen. X is the private key, and Y is computed as Y = G^X mod P. The key's validity period is not in the KEY record. It is indicated by the SIG record that signs the KEY record at that domain name.
sections.eli5: A key is a few big numbers lined up in a fixed order. One small number up front says how big the others are, and the secret number never goes in the phone book.

sections.title: The DSA SIG Record
sections.content:
In a SIG record, the signature part has three fields, in this order: T (1 octet), R (20 octets) and S (20 octets). The fields that come before the signature in the SIG record data are defined in RFC 2535, which also says how the data to be signed is determined.

The signer then follows FIPS 186: take hash = SHA-1 ( data ), pick a random K with 0 < K < Q, and compute R = ( G^K mod P ) mod Q and S = ( K^(-1) * (hash + X*R) ) mod Q. Because Q is 160 bits long, R and S cannot be larger than the 20 octets allocated.

T is copied from the public key. It is not logically necessary in the SIG, but it is there so that values of T above 8 can serve as an escape for extended versions of DSA or other algorithms specified later.
sections.eli5: A signature is two numbers computed from the message and the secret key. Anyone holding the matching public key can check them, and a copy of the size number rides along in case the format changes later.

sections.title: Speed and Size Trade-offs
sections.content:
Signature generation speed is roughly the same for RSA (see RFC 2537) and DSA. With enough pre-computation, DSA signing is faster, and DSA key generation is also faster. Verification is the weak spot: it is an order of magnitude slower than RSA when the RSA public exponent is small, as is recommended for KEY records used to authenticate DNS data.

DNS implementations of the time were optimized for small transfers, typically under 512 bytes including overhead. Larger transfers work, but the RFC advises keeping KEY record sets as small as adequate security allows, remembering that a secure zone also returns at least one authenticating SIG record.
sections.eli5: Making signatures is quick, but checking them takes much longer than with the other main kind. Since the phone book likes small answers, keep keys no bigger than they need to be.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many of the general security considerations in RFC 2535 apply. Keys retrieved from the DNS should not be trusted unless they were securely obtained from a secure resolver or independently verified by the user, and that process meets the user's security policy. How strong a key must be depends on local policy.

The current DSA standard limits keys to a maximum of 1024 bits (T = 8), which may limit security. For particularly critical applications, implementors are encouraged to consider the range of available algorithms and key sizes.

DSA needs frequent, high quality random numbers (see RFC 1750). If manipulated numbers are used instead of random ones, very high bandwidth covert channels are possible, and leaking a whole DSA private key from only two signatures has been demonstrated. DSA is secure only with trusted implementations, including trusted random number generation.
sections.eli5: A signature machine needs a fresh, truly unpredictable number every time. If someone tricks it into using a bad one, the secret key can leak out.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Giving a meaning to any value of the T parameter that this document does not define requires an IETF standards action. The unallocated values are meant to cover future extensions of the Digital Signature Standard (DSS).
sections.eli5: The spare values of the size number are saved for later, and only a formal decision by the standards group can give them a meaning.
